problem: The USB chargeable bike light had stopped charging, so the owner had peeled away the silicon overmoulding the wires. One of the wires was visibly detached from the USB charging connector, so that was soldered on by one of the fixers. This did not seem to have solved the problem, and as the other repairs moved on, the bike light waited for a spare moment to be looked at again. Another fixer picked up the repair and, looking closely, with a loupe, and prodding with a multimeter for the signs of life throught the remaining silicon overmoulding, it was discovered that the other wire connection is corroded. The repairer extended the wire, soldered it to the extension and to the USB charging plate, and the light was now charging and working properly. As the light clips around the handlebar when in use and the USB charging connector is designed as a part of the grip holder, the light will need overmoulding the connections with something like Sugru, something that waterproofs it, providing flexibility and allowing for further repairs if needed. Overall it is a fiddly job, but these lights are comparatively expensive to buy and very good when they work. The 3rd party parts required were wires for the extension and Sugru for overmoulding.
The CD had stopped playing. The repairer examined it, found the switch was stuck, and the whole item needed cleaning. Sprayed and cleaned, and brought the CD player back to life.

This vintage lamp came dissassembled, the base, the bulb socket and wire were all separate and needed wiring. The bulb socket was made of melamine and was puzzling to open. It was successfully wired and lit up to applause and cheers from everyone.

After having worked only for 3 months, the radio stopped working. The repairer checked if it works with batteries, which it did. Then the repairer opened it and inspected the components. Having seen this sort of problem before, the repairer knew to look at the power board. The power board path was interrupted and did not deliver any charge from the plug in cable. The repairer bridged and bypassed the interruption and the radio worked again. The owner was above the moon, saying the radio is like their friend, as they choose to not have a TV, but do listen to radio for news and comfort. They said they used to take out insurance on these items, but it adds up over the time, and this was not the first radio dying in the first months of use.

The participant had two phones of the same model, one of which had a shattered screen, the other had a bad battery life. He wanted to put the good battery into the phone with the good screen. We had a repairer with the right skillset, but did not have the glue needed for replacing the screen. We will source the glue and see if it can be repaired at the next Restart party.
The printer's printing function had stopped, although it was still feeding the paper through sometimes, and was functioning as a scanner. No solution was found.

The printer had stopped communicating with the computer, which is why updating drivers was not possible, if they could be found. A small possiblity that another type of cable could connect to the computer remained, but the owner would have to source the cable and try that on their own.
The iron had a shattered plug casing, but all the connections inside it seemed in good condition. The plug casing would need to be sourced and the repair could be done at the next Restart Party.

It was fixed by putting it together to fit, which needed some bending, glueing and screwing together. It was made to work again. The repairer said the repair is not likely to last due to the flimsy nature of the manufacturing.

The participant needed assistance to undertand and fix why a mic request came up in the texting filed for messages, not the keyboard. It needed a Gboard plug-in keyboard turned on and selected to be a deafult keyboard. Problem was solved. The participant had had the same problem before, and someone else had helped them solve it, but they did not know the root of it.

The hinge above the cupping earpiece had a plastic overmoulding to provide a channel for the cable. This plastic channel had broken. The participant had tried glueing it with a superglue, which did not quite work out. The superglue was scraped off and a plastic weld was applied. It would form an amalgamated seam, and we can consider it fixed, but the seams in plastic are never as strong as original moulding, so it might break again.
The participant wanted to know if the table lamp, made of several types of metal, was safe to touch when on. It was PAT tested and found to be safe.

The participant had bought rechargeable batteries, but although charged, they were not powering the phone. The repairer found that the new batteries are slightly shorter than the old ones had been and bent the contacts to make it work.

The owner had stepped on the tablet and half the screen had stopped working. It was still charging and the other half of the screen with the menu was working, but it was not possible to repair the lower half.

The tamagochi had been opened and resoldered 10 years ago and working after the treatment, bet the fault could not be found this time. Perhaps it would need the same thorough treatment to briing it back to life. It also needed new screws for the back plate to hold the batteries in. The owner had a real affection for their childhood toy pet, and wanted to do anything it would take to bring it back to life.

It was previously looked at the repair shop in Philippenes, where it was suggested that the battery was heating up too much (it was getting too hot to wear). It had already calmed down and there were no other repairs waiting, so the repair volunteer looked at it and gave an assessment that the charging port had melted pins that would need replacing, and the battery was in a good condition. It was opened successfully, and the battery was tested. The exact size and Wattage replacement battery could not be found online as a spare straight away, but the owner of the light said they will try again at home.

One of the earpods was trodden on, making it split along the seam. It had also stopped working. Usually, these are non-repairable as the access is prohibited through design. The battery-operated vibrating device had stopped working. The issue was with the power connection, which was reinforced and secured, preventing it from moving and detaching again.

The device powering the vibration cushion for sensory support had stopped working. It was a small, heart shaped casing with a vibration motor connected to a large push-button, activating it. A component on the microscheme, connecting the batteries to the rest had overloaded and was damaged. There was no way to replace it or repair it, rendering the part obsolete. A replacement part cannot be purchased, and the whole new cushion costs GBP 40. It seems like they work with amazing margins and really cash in on children's disabilities.

L'ordinateur s'éteint ou se fige de manière aléatoire. Il y a des plantages de l'Explorateur Windows (dossier "Téléchargements") et une non-reconnaissance des souris USB. Historique des interventions : Le HDD d'origine a été remplacé par un SSD. Une migration de Windows 10 (22H2 vers 24H2) a été effectuée pour tenter de résoudre les instabilités logicielles. Résultat : La migration n'a rien changé. Les problèmes persistent (figements, USB morts). Diagnostic approfondi et Cause racine : L'analyse révèle une corruption systémique généralisée : HDD Défectueux : Le disque d'origine présente un défaut physique électronique ("toxique" pour le bus USB), provoquant des perturbations électriques qui font planter le système et coupent les ports USB. Transfert du défaut au SSD : Lors de la copie (clonage ou restauration de l'image) des données du HDD vers le SSD, le SSD a hérité de la corruption. Le "contaminant" logiciel (système corrompu) et potentiellement les paramètres de gestion de l'alimentation défectueux sont maintenant présents sur le SSD. Conséquence : Le SSD, bien que physiquement sain, fonctionne avec un système d'exploitation corrompu qui reproduit les mêmes symptômes (plantages, figements, conflits USB) que l'ancien HDD. Plan d'action correctif : - Arrêt immédiat de l'utilisation du HDD défectueux pour éviter d'endommager davantage le matériel.

The waffle iron (my mother's, dating to the 1940s) was disassembled and tested. Preliminarily, since no substitute cords were available, we reinserted the old line into the machine connector. I had already intended to purchase a new cord. The specific electrical requirements of the machine were explained to me, so now I know how to buy the correct cord. We unscrewed the bottom plate, exposing the workings of the lower griddle. When tested, the electrical circuit was fine. The control governing the degree of doneness of the waffle is a completely mechanical thing, running from the knob outside to two little flanges in the middle of the machine which expand or contract with heat. They seemed to be a little stuck (which may account for complaints about overheating). I was advised to sand them down with 600-1200 grit sandpaper to clear the accumulation. I had a lot of questions about cleaning, water, etc. which were answered. So far so good. When we unscrewed the top to expose the upper waffle iron, however, the electrical circuit did not complete. The little white wires leading from the plug to the hot plate part were defective. Diagnosis: the white wires of both top and bottom valves need to be replaced, along with their receptor nuts and bolts; and the heat gauge flanges need to be sanded. It should take an electrical repairman about an hour to do. The going rate for electrical repair in Berkeley is $50-75/ hour. As instructed, I will phone Al Lasher's Electronics on University Avenue for a recommendation.. The decision to restore a vintage electrical appliance is based on many factors. The initial assessment at the clinic establishes an upper limit of feasibility and cost. Beyond that, more personal considerations-- environmental, aesthetic and sentimental-- must be taken into account. How much do I loathe sending things to landfill (or having them sent to landfill by whoever inherits the non functional waffle iron)? A lot. Would a second-hand replacement (say from the Oakland Museum White Elephant Sale) be any safer than an appliance (ungrounded, to be sure) which I had had rewired? No. Do I even need a waffle iron? I've lived thirty years with this one in storage. But so many interesting new whole grain waffle recipes are circulating. Could I find a second-hand stove-top iron? As I see it right now, this is a perfectly good waffle iron which can be fixed with a trivial amount of work. Since I lack the skills to fix it myself I have to pay someone to do it. For people retired on a small fixed income in Berkeley everything is ridiculously expensive. I have suggested several times to the North Berkeley Senior Center that it would be good to maintain a list of retired repairmen who would be willing to undertake occasional work for less than the going rate. I have even suggested a program of exchanged work or skills. I can cook or garden expertly in exchange for a small electrical repair. In vain. The unimaginative management is totally uninterested in improving the lives of its members.

When we arrived, a Volunteer (Tom) showed us how to use a multimeter in order to determine that yes, our lamp had a short. First we checked the cord connections to the bulb socket and re-connected them to make sure they were tight and clean. The multimeter indicated that there was still a problem, though, so we took the lamp apart and found that the entire wire needed replacing. We did this, ensuring that the ground wire and the live wire were consistently threaded throughout. We left happily with a working lamp. First, make sure you have the right tools: screwdriver, wire strippers/cutters, a replacement wire that is the right length and meant to carry the same voltage, and a multimeter, at bare minimum. Our lamp was a floor lamp with a tall, skinny post that the cable went through. I wished I'd had a long, narrow stick that I could poke into that post. Next, take a good look at your lamp and think about how it might come apart. Look for screws, caps, or other joined places that will provide access to the wire inside the lamp. Think about what might be necessary in order to get the wire out (and in). Visualizing the process before you start is a good idea. There's probably a lot of reference on how to go about fixing the wiring on a lamp online, but it was very helpful to have someone guide us through the process. I never would have thought to use a multimeter, but using it as a way of testing our work instead of just plugging the lamp in was a good thing, it avoided potentially shorting the circuit at the event.

problem: It took a long time to figure out how to do so, but two fixers were able to partially dismantle the tape deck, remove the UK transmission, and put the original transmission back into the tape deck. Their comment was "They don't make them like they used to." The job was complicated due to the age of the tape deck and lack of a service manual but worth doing because of the quality of the machine. Thanks to their efforts, the tape deck is now working again. I appreciate the fact that the idea behind Fixit Clinics is to involve participants in repairing their items and to teach people how to carry out repairs. However, I think allowances need to be made for the complexity of the item involved, the age of the item, the experience (or lack thereof) of the owner, and the experience of fixers with older models. I would advise attendees to go to Fixit Clinics with hopes of getting their items repaired but feel that they should not have unrealistic expectations. The fixers are wonderful but there are limits to what they can accomplish.

The microwave turntable wasn't turning, so I had purchased a replacement motor over a year ago and brought it with me to the event. We replaced the motor and now the turntable turns. Yay! Changing the motor was easy, but getting the case/housing off the microwave was challenging. On the bottom of the microwave, there was a covering right over the motor, but we didn't think we could open it since it required cutting metal to do so. To get the case off, we needed a special tool (Security Torx screwdriver, which is a 6-sided star-shaped screwdriver with a pin in it) and luckily (amazingly), someone at the Fixit Clinic had one. We also used a regular Phillips screwdriver. We kept liberating parts of the case and finding that we had to unscrew more screws to get to the area we needed. (Also, it's a bit intimidating working with electric wires and stuff but we just avoided touching those.) After a lot of work, we got the whole case off of the microwave, but none of that was necessary after all. EXCEPT, by opening the case, we found some super secret instructions taped onto the microwave underneath the case, so it DID tell us what to do! It turned out we COULD get in through the covering right over the motor (so we only needed to open that, not take the entire case off). It turned out, you do just cut the metal, open it up, replace the motor, and then rotate the cover 180 degrees and it has tabs that slip into slots so it can be reused after being cut. The motor itself just needed to be unplugged, rotated, and pulled out. Then we plugged in the new one and rotated it into place. Voila! .

Oven intermittently would not heat and turntable wouldn't turn. At repair event the probable issue was determined to be a series of switches that are engaged by the door. Went ahead and ordered a latch hook, PHOK-A137WRFZ, two switches QSW-MA131WRE0 and a switch/fuse combination FFS-BA021WRK0. I removed the latch hook assembly and tested the three switches. They seemed fine. Installed the new latch hook with the new switches, but noticed that this assembly is designed to be adjustable and has "play" while the two screws that hold it aren't tightened. With the door closed, this assembly can be accurately aligned to optimally engage the switches. I did this and then tightened the two screws holding it with the hope they would not move over many years. The system works now without any intermittent failures. When the oven was in a state where it wouldn't start, it could reliably be started after going through one or more cycles of pushing the "open" mechanical button on the front while holding the door closed. This process is referred to in the service manual as helpful in aligning the latch hook. It also exercises the process of engaging the 3 switches on the latch hook and might guide people to this resolution.

Initial issue: intermittently not working and would hum but blades would barely turn or not at all. At the repair event, we took it apart starting with the plastic clips holding the outer "cage". We noticed it was dusty, the main rod attaching to the blades was rusted, and the blades turned but were stiff. I had oiled it at home but not taken it apart. We continued disassembly, next removing the fan blades. They took a firm and steady pull to get off the main pole. Be careful here, because the plastic can crack around where it threads onto the pole. Mine did and we had to glue it. Next, we removed the 2 nuts and washers holding the back of the "cage" onto the fan. From there, the next disassembly was to get the motor out. I wanted to check the electronics and see if anything looked bad. We removed the bolts holding the legs/base and that allowed the motor to slide out. We had to flex the plastic to get it out. there are also 2 metal tabs that the bolts screw into, acting as nuts. make sure not to lose those. Once we pulled out the motor, someone came over to help who was familiar w similar fans. He suggested we lubricate the bearings both at the front and back of the rotating pole. Everything just looked old and rusty, but nothing was super messed up. We used deoxit to lube the parts, and it made a huge difference. We also krazy glued the part of the fan blade assembly that we'd inadvertently broken during disassembly. Lastly, we scraped off some of the rust from the main pole near where the blades attach. When reassembling, make sure the base is pointing in the right direction. Make sure you screw the base bolts into the metal tabs. when reattaching the fan blades, make sure the plastic gaps line up with the little perpendicular metal stoppers that stick out from the pole. After reassembling some, we tested and saw that the fan ran quietly and well. After full reassembly, the same was true. lubing the back bearing was important for long term repair! I lubed only the front initially but it wasn't enough.

The brush roller had stopped spinning, even after I did the regular clearing of all of our dog's fur from the roller etc. Before I visited to the Fix It Clinic at the Sudo Room, I did some googling and learned that there was a small micro-switch in the lower unit of the vacuum that would toggle the brush roller on/off when the vacuum was in the reclined/upright position. This micro-switch would often fail - I bypassed this switch (did not actually test the switch which was a mistake) and the problem persisted. I ordered another lower unit from e-bay hoping that it would either work or could be cannibalized for parts. After it did not work, I signed up for the Fix It Clinic. After submitting the initial report form, I visited the clinic where I was helped by Peter and Jake. They were not only incredibly helpful, but they were also really friendly and encouraging, both of the work I had already done, and continuing to troubleshoot and resolve the issue. We systematically tested the unit, ruling out a burnt out brush roller motor (something I wasn't sure how to test before the clinic) and ultimately we determined that the three position rocker switch that turned on the vacuum + turned on the brush roller was faulty. After ordering a replacement switch online, I was able to install it and reassemble the vacuum and it is in perfect working order and now I feel empowered to work on it myself! At least until I get in over my head, when I will be bringing it back to the Fix It Clinic!. Safety first (duh!) Start with google and youtube - especially if it is a common model - I was able to find a lot of information about the vacuum, including common repair issues. Even though I didn't actually have one of the common challenges. I would not do "irreversible" things like bypassing the micro-switch without being quite or absolutely certain that is the issue. Be patient and take photographs regularly so you can re-assemble. Don't be too forceful disassembling - there are loads of hidden screws and you could easily break the plastic bits. I found when I unscrewed everything things came apart quite easily - if you're forcing something, you've likely missed a screw. If you've exceeded what you're able to do on your own - visit the Fix It Clinic! Show up early, be prepared to stay awhile because 1) they're busy volunteers helping multiple people at a time and 2) it's fun and interesting and you'll meet cool people!

I tried emptying the bin of pencil shavings, checking for lead obstructions, and also replacing the batteries. The repairperson discovered that when the bin was in place and properly seated, one side of it caused a metal piece to contact and complete the first part of the circuit. The second part of the circuit was closed when the pencil was inserted, thereby causing the sharpener blade to spin. However, the issue was that the piece that was contacted by the bin did not function as intended and complete the first part of the circuit. Therefore, the repairperson bent the metal so that it would constantly contact and complete that first part of the circuit. In fact, the pencil sharpener had been faulty to begin with prior to the repair because of inconsistent contact of the metal piece connected to the bin. After shaping the metal component, it now works consistently. Don't be afraid to take it apart and play with the components to understand how they all function together to make the sharpener work. There is a lot of grease inside the sharpener, so make sure that you have some wipes handy after the repair. The repair is also messy from the pencil shavings. It's very important to make note of which parts, screws, and gears you removed and in what sequence. Lastly, replace all screws and gears only after testing to ensure that the sharpener works.

In cases where there are intermittent connectivity issues on wave soldered boards, look for the larger pins which will have poorer solder joints (because wave soldering requires bringing everything up to the same temperature which works well for small pins but larger pins are too big to get hot enough). Using leaded tin solder, re-solder any of these suspect joints (large pins, visual cracks, matte instead of shiny). This may require melting, sucking the solder off with a solder-sucker, and soldering anew, or merely melting and adding some solder)

C'est un four micro onde qui possède également la fonction chaleur tournante. Ce four à la particularité de posséder un clapet amovible situé dans la cavité qui contient la lampe d'éclairage du four, cavité qui est attenante à la chambre de chauffe et qui communique avec celle-ci à travers une grille. Je ne sais pas à quoi sert ce clapet : évacuation de la chaleur ou de l'humidité ? Dans la fonction micro onde ou dans la fonction chaleur tournante ? Je ne sais pas. 

Depuis quelques semaines, le four s'éteint spontanément après une minute exactement, qu'il soit utilisé en fonction micro onde ou en fonction chaleur tournante. Après avoir cherché sur internet, je suis tombé sur quelques article mentionnant que le clapet pouvait être la source du problème. J'ai effectivement remarqué dans un premier temps que le clapet s'ouvrait et se fermait en cours de chauffe (et dans les deux types de fonctions) de façon apparemment erratique. 

J'ai ensuite ouvert le four pour faire quelques tests. Le clapet est surmonté par un moteur rotatif qui le commande, et ce clapet bute sur un détecteur lorsqu'il est dans sa position fermée. 
* En démarrant en mode chaleur tournante, le moteur tourne dans le sens anti-horlogique si la position du clapet au départ est fermée. Si la position de départ est ouvert, alors le moteur tourne dans un des deux sens de manière apparemment aléatoire. Le four s'arrête au bout d'une minute. 
* Si pendant la première minute je ferme le clapet (ou l'ouvre puis le ferme), Alors le moteur s'arrête et le four continue au delà de la minute. 
* En démarrant en mode micro ondes, le moteur tourne dans le sens anti-horlogique si la position du clapet au départ est ouverte. Si la position de départ est fermée, alors le moteur tourne dans un des deux sens de manière apparemment aléatoire. Le four s'arrête au bout d'une minute. 
* Si pendant la première minute je ferme le clapet en partant de la position ouverte, Alors le moteur s'arrête et le four continue au delà de la minute. J'ai le même comportement si je démarre avec le clapet position fermée et que je l'ouvre pendant la première minute. 

Merci d'avance pour votre aide.

Ik verving de beide eindversterkerlampen EL84-type door matched pair lampen van JJ electronics en ook de drie voorversterkerlampen 12AX7-type door Sovtek lampen. Als ik hem nu aanschakel geeft hij enkele seconden lang een normaal volume, maar valt dan terug op een lager volume.. Dat is wel redelijk, maar het geluid wordt bij het hoger instellen van het volume heel snel 'blurry'. Je kan alles schijnbaar blijven gebruiken, maar er komt geen geluid meer uit. Vanaf dan haalt drukken op de power-knop ook niets meer uit, de enige manier is de stekker uittrekken en herbeginnen.
